24 boards measured on one set of tests, side by side.

Bars scale to the best board in each column (control loop on a log scale, as in its chart). Boards with none of these three results are left out. Outlined bars are other vendors' boards; a muted value is an unofficial build, not ranked. Hover a value for the clock and build; each chart below has the rows behind it.

Two things to know before you start. At -O3, where GCC is built with -funroll-loops, TI Arm Clang scores 26% higher than GCC on the MSPM0 G3507. In float code, each chip on its own math unit, the LAUNCHXL-F2800137 runs the control loop 34 times faster than the MSPM0 G3507.

CoreMark per MHz by board

The Cortex-M33 boards score about 1.7 times the Cortex-M0+ boards per clock.

CoreMark per MHz: how much general code a core gets done each clock tick. The same source runs on every board at the clock shown in its hover, the board's top clock unless the chart note says otherwise. TI's compiler builds the TI boards and GCC the others, with no OS unless marked.

Control loops

Control loop: ADC trigger to new PWM value

From 1.33 µs to 448 µs across the boards, in float code: hardware math where the chip has it, software math where it does not, each bar says which. The Cortex-M0+ boards run floating point in software, so none gets under 88.5 µs even with a math accelerator for sine and cosine. TI's fixed-point IQmath library brings the MSPM0 G3507 to 12.3 µs.

One field-oriented control step, timed from the ADC finishing to the new PWM value.

Radio RAM

Radio stack RAM on the LP-EM-CC2340R5

6 of 11 builds fit, including every Bluetooth-only and Zigbee one. 5 do not link at 36 kB of RAM (Bluetooth + TI 15.4 at once; Thread end device, NCP build; Thread end device, CLI build; Thread router, CLI build; Thread router, NCP build). They link at 64 kB on the CC2340R53; none has run there.

Bar = RAM the stack needs. The chip has 36 kB.

RAM the stack needs, from the linker mapcalculated: what a build that did not link would need

10.7 kB left
Thread radio only (RCP)
8.8 kB left

6.2 kB left
Bluetooth, TI's data stream
5.3 kB left
Bluetooth, TI's basic example
5.1 kB left
Zigbee router, logging on
799 B left
Bluetooth + TI 15.4 at once
2.1 kB over
Thread end device, NCP build
7.5 kB over
Thread end device, CLI build
10.0 kB over
Thread router, CLI build
16.0 kB over
Thread router, NCP build
20.7 kB over

Scale 0 to 58 kB; 1 kB = 1,024 bytes. These are TI's configurations as built here. No trimmed build was made, so none is a proven chip limit.

Edge AI

A hardware AI engine against the CPU, same model

The MSPM0 G5187's NPU answers 2 to 22 times faster than its own CPU. The SK-TDA4VM's C7x is 13 to 135 times faster than its A72 cores on the models shown.

The same model built for the accelerator and for the CPU, timed per answer.

Linux boards: their own numbers

A Linux board runs its own tests: boot time, memory bandwidth and latency, model inference, video, Ethernet and storage. Most have no MCU to compare with, so the board sits behind the scorecard toggle. These are its headline numbers. The board page has the conditions and limits of each.

Works ran here and did what it shouldShould work it builds; only naming, packaging or build glue is in the way; hover for whichCould work some of it ran; real porting effort is left; hover for whatNot for this chip the chip or its vendor software cannot; hover for whyNot for this chip not enough RAM for itNot for this chip the chip has no radio for itNot for this chip the vendor offers no software for it on this chipNot for this chip a tool or build problem stopped it, not the chipNot for this chip it stopped on the air; the radio link in the room is the suspect, not the chip (not proven)

Every test, every board

The whole store, by test class; the tests that explain a chart sit under that chart. An empty cell is a gap, not a zero. Variant codes:

CodeMeans
ticlangTI Arm Clang, TI's own compiler
gccGCC, the open-source compiler Zephyr uses
armgnu14GCC 14 from the Arm GNU Toolchain
ti-c2000TI's C2000 compiler
bareno operating system
zephyrunder the Zephyr operating system
o2, o3, os, ozcompiler optimization level: o3 is fastest code, os and oz are smallest
o2unrollZephyr's speed setting: -O2 with loop unrolling. Its menu calls it -O3.
flash, ramwhere the code ran from
c28patchCoreMark patched for the C28x 16-bit byte: unofficial
hw, swmath unit in hardware, or the same math in software
nncbuilt by TI's Neural Network Compiler
c-o3the model as plain C at that optimization level
energytracemeasured with the board's own EnergyTrace probe
eoc, earlycontrol loop timed from the ADC end-of-conversion interrupt, or from the earlier ADC-start interrupt
ramfuncthe interrupt handler copied to RAM
o4, o4s0, o4s5C2000 compiler -O4 with size-against-speed settings 0 or 5
q15, q31, f32FFT in 16-bit fixed point, 32-bit fixed point, or 32-bit float
-32mhz, -4mhzthe same build run at that clock instead of the board's top clock
cli, ccs-mcp, west, uniflash, openocd, dslitethe path or tool used: command line, CCStudio's AI tools, Zephyr's tool, TI's flashers, OpenOCD
register, driverone register write, or the vendor's driver call
(one way)the test has only one way to run it, so the row has no variant code

Method

Each test is a program that reports its own cycle count or time, and a script reads it back from the chip. A benchmark that checks its own answer, such as CoreMark's CRC, the AES known answer or a model's test vectors, gives no number when the check fails. Three runs give a median. A row marked 1 run is a single run, which can be off by whatever the Mac, the supply or the radio did that minute: cycle counts from a self-checking benchmark barely move, wall-clock times and radio latencies move a lot. Every number is a row in the results store with its source file, date, clock and build. The full rules are in the method above.

Calculated numbers. A number read from a board is measured. These are worked out from other numbers, and each says so where it appears:

  • Interrupt response in nanoseconds: the best-case cycle count divided by the clock. The chart note says so; the cycles are measured.
  • The outlined bars in the radio RAM chart, marked "calculated" in its legend: the chip's RAM plus the bytes the linker said a stack that did not link was short.
  • Table cells marked "calc.", computed from other rows:
    • CPU cycles per instruction of a whole program, from its time and an emulator instruction count
    • Deep-learning model: one inference, median wall time
    • Driver current-sense output, cached ADC sample (not a calibrated phase current)
    • Emulated machine speed as per mille of the real machine, 159 meaning 15.9 percent
    • Flash used by an outside project ported to the board, with its shim
    • Host-side code for a radio or sensor: flash and RAM on this host
    • Interpreter speed divided by the pace a typical program needs
    • LVGL demo screen refreshes per second
    • Loop rate with 20 percent of the period free (computed, superseded)
    • Mean CPU cycles to decode one 10 ms LC3 frame
    • Mean CPU cycles to encode one 10 ms LC3 frame (value is the mean; the note holds the worst frame)
    • NPU time against the same graph as NNC CPU code, or against hand-written C
    • RAM left after linking a stack
    • RAM used by an outside project ported to the board, with its shim
    • Signal to error ratio of the 8-bit graph against the float reference
    • Tokens per second of a small language model
    • Touch to changed pixel (computed from measured parts, or measured with a real finger)
    • WebAssembly interpreter slowdown against the same C (20k-iteration loop, instruction counts)
    • WebAssembly interpreter slowdown against the same C (fib 20, instruction counts)

Ranks. Control loop and interrupt ranks use the times drawn in the charts. Boards whose times match at the digits shown share a rank: two boards tied for third both read 3 of 11, and the next is 5.

Probe floors. Current figures come from the kit's own EnergyTrace probe. It reads about 1.5 mA on the MSPM0 L1306 with the chip shut down, so every chip figure on that board is the raw reading minus that floor, and one probe count is about 0.1 mA. Very small currents sit at the edge of what the probe can resolve.

Questions this page raises
Which numbers can I compare straight across boards?
Cycle counts and per-MHz scores from the same build at the same compiler level: CoreMark per MHz with ticlang-bare-o3, interrupt latency bare, the model cells in the "fastest plain-C" chart. Milliseconds and absolute CoreMark depend on the clock, so divide by the MHz first. Rows built a different way on each board are not like for like.
Why is the MSPM0 L1306's sleep current 6.2 µA when the data sheet says 1.0?
The board's own probe reads 1.500 mA with the chip shut down, and that is subtracted from every figure. The 6.2 µA is a mean of 36k samples, at the edge of what the probe can resolve, so the probe is the likely cause of the gap.
Why is the MSPM0 L1306's control step so much slower than the LAUNCHXL-F2800137's?
In clock cycles it is about 30 to 45 times (a mean of 12,851 against 286 to 439). In time it is about 108 to 167 times (401.6 µs against 2.4 to 3.7 µs), because the L1306 runs at 32 MHz and the F2800137 at 120 MHz. The Cortex-M0+ has no floating-point unit, so the same C runs in software float there, while the C28x has an FPU. The F2800137's own software-against-TMU rows show its trig unit adds another 2 times on top.
What does "does not fit" mean, and why does it have a number?
The program linked but needed more RAM than the chip has; the number is how many bytes short, from the linker. It is a build result for one configuration built with local changes, not a measurement on the board.
Why are some radio rows "failed"?
The CC2340R5's Zigbee update from Home Assistant starts and then stops: the best of nine transfers reached 88.74%. Every long transfer ended on lost block replies, which points at the radio environment. Its Bluetooth on TI's Zephyr fork boots but sent nothing on the air. Each has a write-up on its project page.
Why do the two Zigbee "command latency" cells differ by 16 times?
They measure different things: a light being switched (CC2340R5, 95 ms) and a sleepy sensor being read, which waits for the sensor's 3 s poll (CC1354P10-1, 1,574 ms). The difference is in what each row times, not in the chips.
Why is the STOP0 current not the data sheet's 151 µA?
The data sheet measures STOP0 with the main oscillator slowed to 4 MHz. The program left it at 32 MHz, so the 329 µA is a different configuration, not a worse chip.
Why is the LAUNCHXL-F2800137's CoreMark not a score?
CoreMark assumes an 8-bit byte; the C28x core's smallest addressable unit is 16 bits, so three of CoreMark's four self-checks fail unpatched. The patched build runs the same work but is not a certified score. Details in c2000-launchpad/bench/general-benchmarks.md.
Why does CoreMark per MHz on the MSPM0 G3507 drop from 32 MHz to 80 MHz?
Flash cannot answer at 80 MHz without the core waiting; it needs two wait states per flash read, so each iteration takes about 7% more cycles. Code copied to RAM would not pay that.

Sources

  • data/results/<board>.csv: one row per number, with its source file, date, clock and conditions
  • data/benchmark-suite.json: the test list, units and which way is better
  • data/boards.csv: the boards, their cores, clocks and RAM
  • Toolchain for most rows: Intel Mac, macOS 15.7, CCStudio 21.0.1, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1, Zephyr 4.4.2. The variant on each row names anything different.
  • Last measurement 2026-11-10. 1 kB = 1,024 bytes.
